sentences: A woman in a kimono holds a strand of her black hair between her teeth as she turns to look back at us.
Her face is pale, her teeth are blackened, and the hem of her robe and her feet fade away, hinting that she is no longer among the living.
Uemura Shōen drew on the Noh play Aoi no Ue, adapted from The Tale of Genji, in which Lady Rokujō's jealousy turns her into a living spirit that torments her rival.
Her Noh teacher Kongō Iwao told her that the deigan mask has gold in its eyes, so she painted gold onto the back of the silk to make this woman's eyes glint.
Her robe bears wisteria and a spider-web pattern; the web adds to the unsettling mood.
She showed it at the 12th Bunten exhibition in 1918.
Famous for serene, graceful beauties, Shōen later called this her one and only painting of terrible, haunting beauty.
